reasoning: Palestinian adjective wisikh, with the fi3il pattern (i-i), not MSA wasikh. Means dirty.
Reflexive imperative khalli plus -k, so 'keep yourself', with a short i. خير is kheer with ee. Shared Levantine parting phrase, said to a man.
هيك is heek with ee. The article assimilates to د: id-dinya. The dinya/dunya vowel is the uncertain part.
Colloquial silk (plural aslaak) means wire or cable. Palestinians also use the loanword kabl.
The spelling with و shows a long oo. The sigh of annoyance, pain or tiredness is shared across the Levant. The initial hamza is a vowel seat, so nothing is written for it.
Form V verbal noun with a doubled n and short final i, as in ta7addi. It is MSA in origin but used in ordinary talk about the topic. Spoken forms often use the verb tbanna instead.
Geminate -ayy keeps its diphthong (feminine nayye, as in kibbe nayye). The spelling omits the shadda. The vowel quality is my main uncertainty.
Both the hamza after the article and the ق are glottal stops. The glottal is written inside the token, as in il-'usbuu3. 3a plus il- gives 3al-.
Colloquial word for nose (plural mnakhiir, often used even for one nose). The first vowel is i or a depending on the speaker, and I chose i. The formal word anf is not used in conversation.
Means darkness and the dark time after dusk. Taa marbuta after م is e. The syncopated form 3atme is also possible, so the vowel pattern is uncertain.
ص is emphatic, so S. Stress falls on oo and the first long vowel shortens. In Palestinian cooking, plain fasooliya usually means green beans, and dried white beans are fasooliya beeDa or yaabse.
MSA-origin abstract noun used in everyday talk about rights, so it counts as Palestinian. The final ة follows a long aa and is pronounced -aa, as in 7ayaa.
Names the first two letters, used for the alphabet or basics of a subject. The initial alif is a vowel seat, so no glottal is written.
ط is emphatic, so T. Taa marbuta after ب is e in the urban pronunciation.
Palestinian ما plus a verb with the bi- prefix. ص is emphatic, so biSiir. The article elides after illa, giving l-kheer. Common reassurance meaning 'nothing but good will come'.
English loanword used as is. I kept the final th, though some speakers say t or s there. The vowel length in the first syllable may vary.
Classical hayl becomes heel with ee. It is the standard word for cardamom, as in 'ahwe bil-heel. The English spelling 'cardamon' is a typo for cardamom.
First-person past of 3amal is 3amalt. The MSA-loan ث in 7aadith is usually s in urban speech, so I respelled it as س. Some educated speakers say th.

Spoken 'which' before a feminine noun is ayya, and in fast speech bi-ayya sounds like bayya. The glottal after the prefix is written per the rule. Taa marbuta after ع is a. The question mark is not romanized.
ض is emphatic, so D. Pattern fi3aala, like ziyaara, with taa marbuta e after ف. Also means the drinks and food offered to guests.
ث is t in native urban Palestinian numbers (talaata, talaatiin). The ending is -iin.

vowelled_arabic: اللِّي بِيحْفُر حُفْرَة لَأَخُوه بِيقَع فِيها
reasoning: Palestinian present prefix bi-, and the relative اللي is illi. The verb waqa3 is 'a3 in the present, with ق as a glottal stop. The kin term is akhuuh, with la- plus a glottal between prefix and noun.
The standard colloquial word for fan. ح is not in the list of consonants that give final a, so I wrote e by the scheme. Some speakers say mirwa7a.
Palestinian itneen (from ithnayn, with ث as t), not MSA al-ithnayn. Yoom has long oo and neen has ee. The alif of itneen is a connecting alif, so no glottal follows il-.
Standard word for festival, used in Palestine for cultural and music festivals. The stress is on the last syllable, which has a long aa.
